facts.claim: The Bandcamp credits for Killin' Uncle Buzzy say the album was produced by Travis Meadows and Reid Scelza with Barry Dean, and recorded, mixed and mastered by Reid Scelza.
Barry Dean sings background vocals on 'It Gets Better'. He is listed as the special guest vocalist for this track.
'It Gets Better' runs 3:10 and is track 7 of the 10-song album Killin' Uncle Buzzy.
The digital distributor listing (TuneCore, via YouTube) shows a 2011 Independent release dated 2011-07-19, while Bandcamp lists the album as released July 4, 2011.
Meadows wrote the album in 2010 while recovering from alcohol addiction during his fourth stay in rehab.
Meadows says a rehab counselor suggested he keep a journal, and he basically made the record out of that journal.
In his album note, Meadows says the record documents almost seven months of climbing out of a hole he dug for himself. He calls it part exorcism and part killing 'Uncle Buzzy'.
Meadows told American Songwriter that Killin' Uncle Buzzy was the only record he never intended anyone to hear. He described it as his attempt to dig himself out of a hole.
The album was reissued on April 30, 2021 by Earache Records for its 10th anniversary, including a limited clear vinyl edition.

Meadows was born in 1965. He signed with Universal Music Publishing but his addictions kept him from capitalizing on it. He got sober in 2010 and self-released Killin' Uncle Buzzy. His songs have been cut by Dierks Bentley, Eric Church and Jake Owen, among others.

research.lineage: Nashville-based confessional country/Americana singer-songwriter tradition, with the album circulating among Nashville artists as an underground recovery-journal record before Meadows's songs were cut by mainstream country acts.

draft:
**It Gets Better** moves like someone who has finally stopped running. The drums are played with brushes and sit far back, the bass walks instead of pushes, and a fingerpicked acoustic guitar turns its pattern over and over at a slow, easy swing. Travis Meadows sings over it in a clear, mid-range voice, smooth and unhurried, with no strain anywhere. It's a calm song. Once you know where it came from, that calm becomes the whole story.

Meadows wrote *Killin' Uncle Buzzy* in 2010, during his fourth stay in rehab. A counselor suggested he keep a journal, and he says he basically made the record out of it. In his note for the album he describes almost seven months of climbing out of a hole he dug for himself, and calls the record "part exorcism." He later told American Songwriter it was the only record he never meant anyone to hear.

That changes what a title like "It Gets Better" is doing. It isn't advice handed down from the safe side of recovery. It's a promise written from inside the process, by someone who had already tried this three times before. A journal entry can hold hope and doubt on the same page without settling which one wins, and this track carries that kind of hope: steady, quiet, and not yet proven. The arrangement never raises its voice to sell the idea. It just keeps time, which is its own kind of faith.

For a record built from private pages, it doesn't sound like a bedroom demo. Meadows produced it with Reid Scelza, who recorded, mixed and mastered it, along with Barry Dean, who also sings background vocals on this track as a guest. The sound is clean and polished, with a natural sense of room around the players. If anything, the polish makes the song gentler than its backstory, and some listeners may want more grit. The gentleness seems deliberate, though. You don't shout a thing you're still trying to believe.

The song belongs to the Nashville confessional songwriter tradition, where a song is first a place to tell the truth about yourself and only second a product. Meadows, born in 1965, had a Universal Music Publishing deal that his addictions kept him from using. *Killin' Uncle Buzzy* circulated among Nashville artists as an underground recovery record, and his songs went on to be cut by Dierks Bentley, Eric Church and Jake Owen. In 2021 Earache Records reissued it for its tenth anniversary, clear vinyl included, which is a long way to travel for a record meant for no one.

The song sticks because you're listening to a man say a hope out loud before he's earned it, softly enough that you end up holding it with him.
